title: Given an integer array and an integer K, return the K most frequent elements. The answer may be in any order and the algorithm should be better than O(n log n) where possible.
shortTitle: Top K Frequent Elements: HashMap Frequency Plus Min-Heap or Bucket Sort
keyPoints: Step 1 is always the same: build a frequency map from element to count using a HashMap.
Min-heap approach: maintain a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency; evict the smallest when size exceeds K. O(n log K) time.
Bucket-sort approach: place elements into frequency-indexed buckets (0 to n), read from highest bucket. O(n) time.
The min-heap is simpler and streaming-friendly; bucket sort is asymptotically optimal but uses O(n) extra space for buckets.
The heap comparator must order by frequency ascending so the least frequent sits on top and gets evicted.
Reversing the comparator by mistake returns the K least frequent elements instead of the most frequent.
When K is small relative to n, the min-heap is the natural choice; when K can be large, bucket sort is better.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies in a map, then pick the top K with a size-K min-heap or with frequency buckets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Step 1: Frequency map** – count how often each element appears using a `HashMap<Integer, Integer>`.
- **Min-heap approach** – a `PriorityQueue` of size K ordered by frequency ascending; poll the smallest when size > K. O(n log K).
- **Bucket-sort approach** – array of buckets indexed by frequency (0 to n); walk from the highest bucket down, collecting K elements. O(n).
- **Trade-off** – heap is simpler and streaming-friendly; buckets are linear but use O(n) extra space.
- **Comparator** – order by frequency ascending so the least frequent is on top and gets evicted first.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the K most common transaction amounts of the day. First a clerk tallies how many times each amount appeared. Then to pick the top K, he either keeps a small shortlist of size K that always drops the least frequent when it overflows (min-heap), or lines up amounts in buckets labeled by their count and reads from the busiest end (bucket sort).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the Top K frequent elements is a two-stage problem. Stage one is always the same: count frequencies with a HashMap. Stage two is the selection, and you choose between a min-heap and bucket sort.

The min-heap approach maintains a heap of size K ordered by frequency ascending. As you iterate the frequency map, offer each key into the heap and evict the smallest when the size exceeds K. After processing all keys, the heap holds the K most frequent. This is O(n log K) and is ideal when K is small. The bucket-sort approach places elements into frequency-indexed buckets and reads from the highest down, achieving O(n) but using an O(n) bucket array.

The critical detail is the heap comparator: order by frequency ascending so the least frequent is on top and gets evicted. Reversing it returns the K least frequent instead.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, the teller app uses this to show a quick-select menu of the most common transaction amounts. In practice K is small (top 5), so the min-heap is the natural fit.

Remember one sentence: Count frequencies with a HashMap, then select the top K using a size-K min-heap in O(n log K) or frequency buckets in O(n).
